prompt: A user sees the planner in the list of recent apps. What can the developer conclude about its process?

choices.text: It is running in the background
choices.why: It may be, and it may also be suspended or gone.

choices.text: It is suspended, because every app in the list is
choices.why: Some are, some still run briefly, and some have no process at all.

choices.text: Nothing: it may be running, frozen, or killed
choices.why: Right. The list shows a picture of the screen in every case.

choices.text: It is still active, only hidden behind the list
choices.why: Active means in front and receiving touches.

prompt: Match each state of the course's model to what is true in it.

pairs.right: visible, with something in front of it
not visible, may still run briefly

right_distractors: running, but only on the server

prompt: Why does the system freeze and kill apps that the user did not close?

choices.text: To keep memory and battery for the app in front
choices.why: Right. The foreground has priority, and the rest give way when it needs room.

choices.text: Because the stores require it
choices.why: It is the operating system's own management, not a store rule.

choices.text: To punish apps that crash
choices.why: Healthy apps are frozen and killed just the same.

choices.text: To install system updates in the background while the phone is idle
choices.why: Updates are not the reason the lesson gives.

prompt: Which moves of the model happen without any callback on either platform?

choices.text: Launching and leaving
choices.why: Launching calls onCreate and the rest; leaving calls onStop or reports .background.

choices.text: Interrupting and resuming
choices.why: Those are onPause and onResume, .inactive and .active.

choices.text: Returning from the background
choices.why: Android calls onRestart, onStart and onResume.

choices.text: Being suspended, and being killed
choices.why: Right. No code runs to be told, so nothing is said.

prompt: Put Android's callbacks in the order an Activity receives them, from launch until it is no longer visible.
The system kills a stopped app's process to free memory. Which callback runs?

choices.text: onDestroy
choices.why: The reference says the process can be killed without calling it, or any other.

choices.text: None
choices.why: Right. After a killable method returns, the process may die without another line of its code.

choices.text: onPause, again
choices.why: onPause already ran on the way out; nothing runs again.

choices.text: onSaveInstanceState, and then onDestroy
choices.why: Nothing runs at the kill itself.

prompt: When does onDestroy run?

choices.text: Every time the app goes to the background
choices.why: That is onStop.

choices.text: When the Activity finishes, or is rebuilt for a configuration change
choices.why: Right, for example going back from it, or rotating the phone; not when the process is killed for memory.

choices.text: Just before the system kills the process to free memory for other apps
choices.why: That is exactly the case where it does not run.

choices.text: When a phone call arrives
choices.why: A call pauses and stops the Activity; it does not destroy it.

prompt: What does Android kill to free memory: an Activity, or a process?

choices.text: The Activity that uses the most memory
choices.why: The guide says the system never kills an Activity directly for memory.

choices.text: Only the Activity's views, keeping its data
choices.why: Nothing is kept: everything in the process goes.

choices.text: Whichever the user chose in Settings
choices.why: The user can kill an app there, but that is not the system freeing memory.

choices.text: The process, with everything in it
choices.why: Right: every Activity, variable and loaded list at once.

prompt: A developer saves the user's draft to a database in onPause, and sometimes it is incomplete. What does Android's lifecycle guide say?

choices.text: onPause is very brief; heavy shutdown work belongs in onStop
choices.why: Right. The guide says onPause may not leave enough time for save operations.

choices.text: Saving is only allowed in onDestroy
choices.why: onDestroy may never run; it is the worst place.

choices.text: Databases cannot be written from a callback
choices.why: They can; the problem is the time onPause allows.

choices.text: The draft should be sent to a server in onPause instead
choices.why: The guide names network calls among the things not to do there.

prompt: Which scenePhase value does a SwiftUI app see when a system alert appears over it?

choices.text: .background
choices.why: The app is still visible.

choices.text: .suspended
choices.why: There is no such phase; a suspended app runs no code to observe one.

choices.text: .inactive
choices.why: Right. In the foreground, but paused.

choices.text: .active
choices.why: Something is in front of it now.

prompt: Why does scenePhase have no value for suspended?

choices.text: A suspended app runs no code that could read it
choices.why: Right. A value nobody can observe would never be seen.

choices.text: iOS never suspends apps
choices.why: Apple's guide says UIKit suspends an app shortly after it enters the background.

choices.text: SwiftUI reports suspension as .background
choices.why: Background is reported before suspension; suspension itself is silent.

choices.text: Suspension is reported through applicationWillTerminate
choices.why: That method is generally not called for apps that support the background.

prompt: A React Native app listens to AppState. On which platform can it receive inactive?

choices.text: Android only
choices.why: The other way round.

choices.text: Both
choices.why: React Native documents inactive for iOS alone.

choices.text: iOS only
choices.why: Right, during transitions and interruptions such as an incoming call.

choices.text: Neither: AppState has only active and background
choices.why: It has three values; the third is inactive.

prompt: Apple's guide and Android's guide differ on the first moment to save user data. How?

choices.text: Apple says to save at termination, Android at onPause
choices.why: Termination is generally not called, and Android advises against saving in onPause.

choices.text: Apple asks already on deactivation; Android points to onStop
choices.why: Right. iOS: save on the move to inactive. Android: onPause is too brief, so onStop.

choices.text: They agree exactly
choices.why: They agree on the background as the limit, not on the first moment.

choices.text: Apple asks at onStop; Android at .inactive
choices.why: The names are swapped between the platforms.

prompt: Match each state of the model to its name on Android.
In the afternoon that lifecycle.ts plays, how many moves print nothing for all three platforms?
node lifecycle.ts launch interrupt leave kill return stops with REFUSED. Why does the model refuse return?

choices.text: return must come before kill
choices.why: Order is not the rule; the state is.

choices.text: return is not one of the model's events
choices.why: It is; it is allowed from background or suspended.

choices.text: The user is not allowed to return during a call
choices.why: There is no call in that sequence.

choices.text: After a kill there is no process to return to
choices.why: Right. A killed app can only be launched again.

prompt: When Ana taps the icon after the kill, Android calls onCreate. What does that tell the app about her afternoon?

choices.text: That she was on a call
choices.why: Nothing about the call reaches the new process.

choices.text: That the previous process was killed for memory
choices.why: onCreate is the same callback as the very first launch.

choices.text: Nothing, unless the app wrote something down on the way out
choices.why: Right. It looks like the first run ever; what was saved is all that survives.

choices.text: Everything, because Android restores the old memory
choices.why: The old process's memory is gone with it.

prompt: Why does an app that never saves its state often seem to work on the developer's phone?

choices.text: The phone has memory to spare, and the developer comes back quickly
choices.why: Right. The common interruption pauses and stops; the kill comes with less memory and longer absences.

choices.text: Development builds are never killed
choices.why: The system does not spare them; the conditions are just kind.

choices.text: The debugger saves and restores the app's state on its own, behind the scenes
choices.why: No such thing is described.

choices.text: Calls never happen on test phones
choices.why: A call does not kill the app anyway; it pauses and stops it.

prompt: In the model, kill may happen from background or from ___, and never from active.
Where does the lesson say to save the half-typed session?

choices.text: In onDestroy or applicationWillTerminate
choices.why: Neither runs when a suspended app is killed.

choices.text: Once a minute, on a timer
choices.why: A timer does not run in a suspended app, and misses the last minute anyway.

choices.text: When the user presses a Save button
choices.why: The user cannot know the system is about to kill the app.

choices.text: On the way to the background
choices.why: Right: onStop, .background, or AppState becoming background.

prompt: Which of these are reliable last moments to save, according to the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: onStop on Android
choices.why: Yes: after it, the process may die unheard.

choices.text: scenePhase becoming .background on iOS
choices.why: Yes, with .inactive as the earlier moment Apple asks for.

choices.text: AppState changing to background in React Native
choices.why: Yes: the same moment, reported to JavaScript.

choices.text: onDestroy on Android
choices.why: It does not run when the process is killed for memory.

choices.text: The root component unmounting in React Native
choices.why: No code runs in a killed process to unmount anything.

prompt: Why does the lesson say to save little on the way out?

choices.text: Because the disk is nearly full
choices.why: Disk space is not the reason given.

choices.text: Because the time there is short and not the app's to extend
choices.why: Right. Uploads and large rewrites belong to work the system agrees to run.

choices.text: Because saving drains the battery
choices.why: A small save costs little; the issue is time.

choices.text: Because the stores reject apps that write too much data on the way out
choices.why: No store rule is involved.

prompt: A React Native app saves its draft in a cleanup function that runs when its root component unmounts. Testers who close the app by hand see it work. What happens to a user whose app is killed while suspended?

choices.text: The cleanup runs late, the next time the app opens
choices.why: Nothing from the old process runs again; the new one starts fresh.

choices.text: The draft is lost: no code ran to unmount anything
choices.why: Right. The save belonged on the move to background.

choices.text: The draft is saved, because React Native unmounts before every kill
choices.why: React Native has no value, and no code, at the kill.

choices.text: The system shows the user a dialog to save first
choices.why: The user is not asked; the kill is silent.

prompt: A user writes a session, gets a call, answers it and talks for an hour while playing a game on speaker. Coming back, the draft is gone. Which step lost it?

choices.text: The call, which killed the app as it arrived
choices.why: A call pauses and stops; it does not kill.

choices.text: Coming back, which reloaded a fresh copy of the app from the store
choices.why: Coming back launched it again; the loss came before.

choices.text: onDestroy, which deletes drafts
choices.why: onDestroy deletes nothing, and did not run here at all.

choices.text: A silent kill while suspended, with nothing saved on the way out
choices.why: Right. The game needed memory, and the app had not written the draft down.

prompt: Put what happens to the planner in order, from the moment Ana goes home to the moment she opens it again after a kill.
items: background: onStop, .background; the draft is saved
